lessons.title: Acids, bases, pH and neutralisation
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Acids, bases, pH, neutralisation, preparation of salts, tests for ions and gases (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define acids, bases and alkalis in terms of H⁺ and OH⁻.
Use indicators and the pH scale.
Write equations for the reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates.
Explain neutralisation and give everyday uses.
reviewNotes: pH values in the bar chart are approximate typical values (gastric juice about 1–2, lemon juice about 2, soap about 10, bleach about 12–13).
Strong/weak acid distinction is based on degree of ionisation; no numerical Ka is required at this level.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Acids and bases
blocks.md: An **acid** produces **hydrogen ions H⁺** in water (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, ethanoic acid). A **base** is a substance that neutralises an acid (metal oxides and hydroxides); a base that dissolves in water is an **alkali** and produces **hydroxide ions OH⁻** (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂, ammonia solution). **Neutralisation**: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

blocks.title: Indicators and pH
blocks.md: **pH scale**: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline. Universal indicator: red/orange (strong acid) → yellow → green (7) → blue → purple (strong alkali). **Litmus**: red in acid, blue in alkali. **Methyl orange**: red in acid, yellow in alkali. **Phenolphthalein**: colourless in acid, pink in alkali. A **strong** acid (HCl, H₂SO₄) is fully ionised; a **weak** acid (ethanoic acid) is only partly ionised.

blocks.title: Reactions of acids
blocks.md:
- acid + metal → salt + hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
- acid + base (oxide/hydroxide) → salt + water: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O
- acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

Salt names: hydrochloric acid → **chlorides**; sulphuric → **sulphates**; nitric → **nitrates**.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- A strong acid is not the same as a concentrated acid: strength is about ionisation, concentration is about how much is dissolved.
- Copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute acids.
- Never taste or touch strong acids and alkalis; wear eye protection.

blocks.caption: Approximate pH of some familiar substances: acids below 7, alkalis above 7.
blocks.alt: A bar chart of pH: stomach acid about 2, lemon juice about 2.5, pure water 7, soap about 10 and bleach about 12.5.

blocks.title: Example 1 — zinc and acid
blocks.statement: Write the balanced equation (with state symbols) for zinc reacting with dilute sulphuric acid and name the products.
steps: Zinc is above hydrogen in the reactivity series so it reacts with dilute acid and forms a salt and hydrogen.
Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g): zinc sulphate and hydrogen.

blocks.title: Example 2 — antacid sum
blocks.statement: How much calcium carbonate neutralises 0.10 mol of hydrochloric acid (CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂), and what volume of CO₂ is released? (Ca 40, C 12, O 16; 24 dm³ per mole)
steps: Ratio CaCO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2, so n(CaCO₃) = 0.10 ÷ 2 = 0.05 mol; mass = 0.05 × 100 = 5.0 g.

lessons.title: Preparing salts
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Acids, bases, pH, neutralisation, preparation of salts, tests for ions and gases (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the solubility rules for common salts.
Describe the preparation of a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base, metal or carbonate.
Describe the preparation by titration and by precipitation.
Calculate the mass of crystals obtained.
reviewNotes: Solubility rules are the standard school set; calcium sulphate and calcium hydroxide are only slightly soluble.
Hydrated copper(II) sulphate CuSO₄·5H₂O has Mr = 160 + 5 × 18 = 250.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Solubility rules
blocks.md:
- All **sodium, potassium and ammonium** salts are soluble.
- All **nitrates** are soluble.
- **Chlorides** are soluble except silver chloride and lead(II) chloride.
- **Sulphates** are soluble except barium sulphate and lead(II) sulphate (calcium sulphate is slightly soluble).
- **Carbonates** and **hydroxides** are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium (and ammonium).

blocks.title: Method A — insoluble base, metal or carbonate in excess
blocks.md:
1. Warm the dilute acid and add the solid **in excess** until no more dissolves.
2. **Filter** off the excess solid.
3. Heat the filtrate to evaporate part of the water (crystallisation point).
4. Leave to cool and crystallise; filter and dry the crystals between filter papers.

Example: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.

blocks.title: Method B and C
blocks.md: **Titration** (for soluble bases such as NaOH, and for Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ salts): find the exact volume of acid that neutralises a known volume of alkali with an indicator, repeat **without** indicator and crystallise. **Precipitation** (for insoluble salts): mix two soluble solutions, filter the precipitate, wash with distilled water and dry. Example: lead(II) nitrate + sodium iodide → lead(II) iodide (yellow ppt) + sodium nitrate.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Add the solid in **excess**, so that all the acid is used up.
- Do not evaporate to dryness: it destroys the crystals; stop when crystals begin to form on a glass rod.
- Filter paper after use should be rinsed; wear eye protection when heating acid.

blocks.caption: Preparing a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble solid in excess: react, filter, evaporate and crystallise.
blocks.alt: Three boxes in a row joined by arrows: acid plus excess solid, filter, and evaporate then crystallise.

blocks.title: Example 1 — copper(II) sulphate
blocks.statement: Describe how to make crystals of copper(II) sulphate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulphuric acid, and find the maximum mass of CuSO₄·5H₂O from 8.0 g of CuO (Cu 64, O 16, S 32, H 1).
steps: Warm the acid, add CuO until in excess (black solid remains), filter, evaporate to crystallisation point, cool, filter and dry.

blocks.title: Example 2 — precipitation
blocks.statement: Choose reagents to prepare insoluble silver chloride and write the ionic equation.
steps: Silver chloride is insoluble: mix two soluble salts, silver nitrate (all nitrates soluble) and sodium chloride solution.
Filter, wash and dry the white precipitate. Ionic equation: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).

lessons.title: Tests for gases, cations and anions
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Acids, bases, pH, neutralisation, preparation of salts, tests for ions and gases (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the tests and results for hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, ammonia and chlorine.
Identify cations using sodium hydroxide solution.
Identify chloride, sulphate, carbonate and nitrate ions.
Plan a simple analysis of an unknown salt.
reviewNotes: Colours of hydroxide precipitates (Cu²⁺ light blue, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ red-brown) and their behaviour in excess NaOH follow the usual school tables; check against the Board's reference list.
Nitrate test (aluminium with sodium hydroxide, heated, gives ammonia) is included as the usual O-level test.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Tests for gases
blocks.md:
- **Hydrogen**: lighted splint → squeaky pop.
- **Oxygen**: glowing splint relights.
- **Carbon dioxide**: limewater turns milky.
- **Ammonia**: turns damp red litmus blue; pungent smell.
- **Chlorine**: bleaches damp litmus paper (turns it white); pale green gas.

blocks.title: Tests for cations (add NaOH solution drop by drop, then excess)
blocks.md:
- **Cu²⁺**: light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess.
- **Fe²⁺**: green precipitate; **Fe³⁺**: red-brown precipitate (both insoluble in excess).
- **Ca²⁺**: white precipitate, insoluble in excess.
- **Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, Pb²⁺**: white precipitate that **dissolves** in excess NaOH (Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ also with ammonia: Zn²⁺ dissolves, Al³⁺ does not).
- **NH₄⁺**: no precipitate; warming gives ammonia gas.

blocks.title: Tests for anions
blocks.md:
- **Chloride Cl⁻**: add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate → white precipitate.
- **Sulphate SO₄²⁻**: add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride → white precipitate.
- **Carbonate CO₃²⁻**: add dilute acid → fizzing, CO₂ turns limewater milky.
- **Nitrate NO₃⁻**: warm with aluminium foil and sodium hydroxide → ammonia (turns damp red litmus blue).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Always add the acid **before** silver nitrate or barium chloride, to remove carbonates that would also give white precipitates.
- Say 'dissolves in excess' only if the precipitate disappears; Ca²⁺ and Al³⁺ both give white precipitates, so use the excess test to tell them apart.

items.text: colour of hydroxide precipitates with NaOH(aq)

blocks.caption: Colours of the precipitates formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to solutions of some metal ions.
blocks.alt: Four test tubes showing precipitates: blue for copper, green for iron(II), orange-brown for iron(III) and white/grey for calcium.

blocks.title: Example 1 — unknown solution
blocks.statement: A solution gives a light blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide, insoluble in excess, and a white precipitate with acidified barium chloride. Identify the salt.
steps: Light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess: Cu²⁺ ions.
White precipitate with acidified barium chloride: SO₄²⁻ ions. The salt is copper(II) sulphate, CuSO₄.

blocks.title: Example 2 — white solid
blocks.statement: A white solid fizzes with dilute acid giving a gas that turns limewater milky. Its solution gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that stays in excess. Which compound is it?
steps: Fizzing with a gas that turns limewater milky: carbonate ion CO₃²⁻.
White precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH: calcium ions Ca²⁺. The solid is calcium carbonate.
